stem: Which element in the first row of the d block is NOT a transition element?

options.rationale: Correct: its only ion, Zn²⁺, has a full 3d¹⁰ sub-shell.
Ti³⁺ is [Ar] 3d¹, an incomplete d sub-shell, so titanium is a transition element.
Cu²⁺ is [Ar] 3d⁹, so copper is a transition element even though the atom is 3d¹⁰ 4s¹.
Ni²⁺ is [Ar] 3d⁸, an incomplete d sub-shell.

explanation: A transition element forms at least one stable ion with an incomplete d sub-shell. Scandium (Sc³⁺, 3d⁰) and zinc (Zn²⁺, 3d¹⁰) do not.

stem: What is the electron configuration of the Cr³⁺ ion?

options.rationale: Correct: Cr is [Ar] 3d⁵ 4s¹; the 4s electron and two 3d electrons are removed.
The 4s electrons are lost before the 3d electrons, not kept.
This keeps a 4s electron; ions lose all their 4s electrons first.
This has lost only the 4s electron: it is the configuration of Cr⁺.

explanation: Cr: [Ar] 3d⁵ 4s¹. Remove the 4s electron, then two 3d electrons: Cr³⁺ is [Ar] 3d³.

stem: Which gaseous ion has the greatest number of unpaired electrons?

options.rationale: 3d⁹ has only one unpaired electron.
3d⁸ has two unpaired electrons.
Correct: 3d⁵, one electron in each of the five d orbitals, so five unpaired.
3d³ has three unpaired electrons.

explanation: Electrons occupy d orbitals singly before pairing (Hund's rule): d⁵ gives the maximum of five unpaired electrons.

stem:
Which of the statements help to explain why the first-row transition elements show variable oxidation states?

1. The 3d and 4s electrons have similar energies.
2. Successive ionisation energies rise gradually while 3d and 4s electrons are removed.
3. The atoms of every transition element have a full 3d sub-shell.

options.rationale: Statement 3 is false: only copper among Ti-Cu has a full 3d sub-shell in the atom.
Correct: similar energies mean no sudden large jump in ionisation energy until the 3d and 4s electrons are used up.
Statement 1 is true, and statement 3 is false.
Statement 2 is also true; it is the ionisation-energy evidence for statement 1.

explanation: Because 3d and 4s are close in energy, different numbers of electrons can be lost or used in bonding; the ionisation energies show no huge jump until the core is reached.
hints: Check statement 3 against the configuration of titanium.

stem: Which description fits the 3dz² orbital?

options.content: four lobes lying in the xy plane, pointing between the x and y axes
options.rationale: This describes the 3dxy orbital.

options.content: four lobes lying in the xy plane, pointing along the x and y axes
options.rationale: This describes the 3dx²−y² orbital.

options.content: a single sphere of density centred on the nucleus, larger than 3s
options.rationale: A sphere describes an s orbital, not a d orbital.

options.content: two lobes along the z axis and a ring of density in the xy plane
options.rationale: Correct: the dz² orbital is unique in having a ring (doughnut) around its middle.

explanation: 3dz²: two lobes on the z axis plus a torus in the xy plane. 3dxy: four lobes between the x and y axes.
hints: Only one d orbital has a ring.

stem: Why does the atomic radius change very little from titanium to copper?

options.content: The nuclear charge stays the same across the series, so the pull on the electrons is the same.
options.rationale: The nuclear charge rises by one with each element.

options.content: Extra 3d electrons shield the 4s electrons, roughly balancing the rising nuclear charge.
options.rationale: Correct: each added electron enters an inner sub-shell, so the outer 4s electrons feel a nearly constant pull.

options.content: Each extra electron enters the 4s sub-shell, which is already full in every atom.
options.rationale: The extra electrons go into 3d, not 4s.

options.content: The metallic bonding gets weaker, so the atoms move further apart.
options.rationale: Bonding strength does not explain the size of isolated atoms.

explanation: Across Ti-Cu each step adds a proton and a 3d electron. The 3d electron shields the 4s electrons fairly effectively, so the effective nuclear charge on them and the radius hardly change.
hints: Which sub-shell receives the extra electron each time?

stem:
The first four ionisation energies of a Period 4 element **Q** are 661, 1310, 2720, 4170 kJ mol⁻¹. Data for three other Period 4 elements (kJ mol⁻¹):

| element | IE₁ | IE₂ | IE₃ | IE₄ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| potassium | 418 | 3070 | 4600 | 5860 |
| scandium | 632 | 1240 | 2390 | 7110 |
| zinc | 908 | 1730 | 3828 | 5980 |

Which element is **Q**?

options.rationale: Potassium's big jump is at IE₂: it has only one outer electron.
Scandium's data show a big jump at IE₄ (three outer electrons).
Correct: no large jump up to IE₄, so four electrons (3d² 4s²) can be removed before the argon core.
Zinc's IE₁ (908) is far higher than Q's (661).

explanation: Q loses four electrons without breaking into the core, so it has four 3d and 4s electrons: titanium, [Ar] 3d² 4s², which shows a highest oxidation state of +4.
hints: Look for where each element's large jump comes.
Q has no large jump among its first four values.

stem:
Which statements correctly compare iron with calcium?

1. Iron has the higher melting point.
2. Iron has the higher density.
3. Iron has the larger atomic radius.

options.rationale: Statement 3 is false: iron's metallic radius is much smaller than calcium's.
Statement 1 is true and statement 3 is false.
Statement 2 is also true: iron is about five times as dense as calcium.
Correct: iron atoms are smaller, so statement 3 is false.

explanation: Iron: stronger metallic bonding (3d and 4s electrons delocalised) gives a higher melting point; heavier, smaller atoms give a higher density; a larger effective nuclear charge gives a smaller radius.
hints: Iron has a larger nuclear charge and poorly shielding 3d electrons.

stem: Which of these ions is NOT paramagnetic?

options.rationale: 3d¹ has one unpaired electron, so it is paramagnetic.
Correct: [Ar] 3d⁰ has no unpaired electrons.
3d² has two unpaired electrons, so it is paramagnetic.
3d⁹ has one unpaired electron, so it is paramagnetic.

explanation: Paramagnetism needs unpaired electrons. Sc³⁺ (3d⁰) and Zn²⁺ (3d¹⁰) have none.

stem: How many unpaired electrons are there in a gaseous Co²⁺ ion?
explanation: Co is [Ar] 3d⁷ 4s²; Co²⁺ is [Ar] 3d⁷. Five d orbitals: five electrons singly, then two pair up, leaving 3 unpaired.
workedSolution: 1. Co is [Ar] 3d⁷ 4s²; Co²⁺ is [Ar] 3d⁷. Five d orbitals: five electrons singly, then two pair up, leaving 3 unpaired.

stem: The first three ionisation energies of vanadium are 648, 1370, 2870 kJ mol⁻¹. Calculate the energy, in kJ mol⁻¹, needed to convert one mole of gaseous vanadium atoms into gaseous V³⁺ ions.
explanation:
1. V(g) → V³⁺(g) + 3e⁻ needs IE₁ + IE₂ + IE₃.
2. 648 + 1370 + 2870 = 4888 kJ mol⁻¹.
3. Using IE₃ alone (2870) gives only the energy for V²⁺ → V³⁺.
workedSolution:
1. 1. V(g) → V³⁺(g) + 3e⁻ needs IE₁ + IE₂ + IE₃.
2. 648 + 1370 + 2870 = 4888 kJ mol⁻¹.
3. Using IE₃ alone (2870) gives only the energy for V²⁺ → V³⁺.
hints: Three electrons are removed one after another.

stem: The first two ionisation energies of manganese are 716 and 1510 kJ mol⁻¹. Calculate the energy, in kJ, needed to convert 2.00 g of gaseous manganese atoms into gaseous Mn²⁺ ions, to three significant figures. (Ar: Mn 54.9)
explanation:
1. Energy per mole for Mn(g) → Mn²⁺(g) = 716 + 1510 = 2226 kJ mol⁻¹.
2. n(Mn) = 2.00 ÷ 54.9 = 0.0364 mol.
3. Energy = 0.0364 × 2226 = 81.1 kJ. Using IE₂ alone gives 55.0 kJ; forgetting to convert to moles gives 2226 kJ.
workedSolution:
1. 1. Energy per mole for Mn(g) → Mn²⁺(g) = 716 + 1510 = 2226 kJ mol⁻¹.
2. n(Mn) = 2.00 ÷ 54.9 = 0.0364 mol.
3. Energy = 0.0364 × 2226 = 81.1 kJ. Using IE₂ alone gives 55.0 kJ; forgetting to convert to moles gives 2226 kJ.
hints: First find the energy per mole, then the amount in 1.00 g.

stem: Copper is a transition element even though a copper atom has a full 3d sub-shell.
explanation: True. The definition is about ions: Cu²⁺ is [Ar] 3d⁹, an incomplete d sub-shell.

stem: Match each characteristic property of transition elements with an example of it.

right.content: manganese in MnO₄⁻ and in Mn²⁺

explanation: Calcium oxide is white: calcium (an s-block metal) shows none of the four properties.

stem: Complete the electron configurations of nickel and of the Ni²⁺ ion.
explanation: Ni (Z = 28): [Ar] 3d⁸ 4s². The ion loses the two 4s electrons: [Ar] 3d⁸.

stem: Name the element of the first d-block row that forms only a 3+ ion, with an empty d sub-shell.
explanation: Scandium forms only Sc³⁺, [Ar] 3d⁰, so it is a d-block element but not a transition element.
hints: It is the first element of the row.

stem: Scandium and zinc are d-block elements. Explain why neither is classed as a transition element.

points.description: Definition: a transition element forms at least one stable ion with an incomplete d sub-shell
Scandium forms only Sc³⁺, [Ar] 3d⁰ (empty d sub-shell)
Zinc forms only Zn²⁺, [Ar] 3d¹⁰ (full d sub-shell)

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: A transition element must form at least one stable ion with a partly filled d sub-shell. Scandium's only ion is Sc³⁺, [Ar] 3d⁰, with an empty d sub-shell, and zinc's only ion is Zn²⁺, [Ar] 3d¹⁰, with a full one, so neither qualifies.

explanation: The test is the ion, not the atom.
hints: Write the configuration of the only ion each element forms.

stem: The first ionisation energy rises steeply across Period 3 (Na to Ar) but changes little across the transition elements (Ti to Cu). Explain the difference.

points.description: Across Period 3 each added electron enters the same outer shell, which gives little extra shielding, so the effective nuclear charge rises and electrons are held more tightly
Across Ti-Cu each added electron enters the inner 3d sub-shell
The 3d electrons shield the outer 4s electrons, roughly cancelling the extra proton, so the attraction for the 4s electron hardly changes

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: In Period 3 the extra electron goes into the same outer shell as the others, so it shields poorly; the rising nuclear charge pulls the outer electrons in more strongly and IE₁ rises. From titanium to copper the extra electron goes into the inner 3d sub-shell, where it shields the 4s electrons that are removed first. The increase in nuclear charge is almost balanced by this shielding, so IE₁ changes little.

explanation: Inner 3d electrons shield the outer 4s electrons.
hints: Which electron is removed first in a transition metal atom?

stem: Explain why iron has a much higher melting point and a much higher density than calcium.

points.description: Iron can delocalise both 3d and 4s electrons (more delocalised electrons per atom than calcium's two 4s electrons)
So the metallic bonding in iron is stronger and more energy is needed to melt it
Iron atoms are smaller than calcium atoms (larger nuclear charge, poor shielding by 3d), so they pack more closely
Iron atoms are also heavier (Ar 55.8 against 40.1), so more mass is packed into each unit volume

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: In iron both the 4s and some 3d electrons are delocalised, so there are more delocalised electrons attracting the cations than in calcium, which has only its two 4s electrons. The metallic bonding is stronger and the melting point higher. Iron atoms are both heavier and smaller than calcium atoms, so more mass is packed into each cubic centimetre and the density is higher.

explanation: Melting point depends on the strength of the metallic bonding; density on atomic mass and atomic size.
hints: Melting point: bonding. Density: mass and size of the atoms.

stem: The first four ionisation energies of a Period 4 element **X** are 653, 1590, 2990, 4770 kJ mol⁻¹. **X** forms a yellow anion XO₄²⁻ and a green aqueous ion X³⁺. Its atoms have a half-filled 3d sub-shell.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Complete the electron configuration of an atom of **X**.
parts.explanation: X is chromium: [Ar] 3d⁵ 4s¹ (half-filled 3d with one 4s electron is the lower-energy arrangement).

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the energy, in kJ mol⁻¹, needed to form one mole of gaseous X³⁺ ions from gaseous X atoms.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Give the electron configuration of the X³⁺ ion, in the form [Ar] 3dⁿ (type it as, for example, [Ar] 3d4).

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: How many unpaired electrons does an X³⁺ ion have?
parts.explanation: 3d³: three electrons in three different d orbitals.
parts.workedSolution: 1. 3d³: three electrons in three different d orbitals.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: In XO₄²⁻ the oxidation state of X is +6. Explain why X can reach this oxidation state but calcium cannot exceed +2.

points.description: X has six 3d and 4s electrons of similar energy, all of which can be used in bonding (to oxygen)
Calcium has only two electrons outside a noble-gas core; removing a third (from 3p) needs far too much energy

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Chromium has six electrons in the 3d and 4s sub-shells, which are close in energy, so all six can be involved in bonding to oxygen in CrO₄²⁻. Calcium has only two electrons outside its argon core; a third would have to come from the 3p sub-shell, which needs a very large ionisation energy.

parts.label: (f)
parts.stem: Which property of the X³⁺ ion depends on its partly filled d sub-shell?

options.rationale: The charge depends on how many electrons are lost, not on the d sub-shell being partly filled.

options.content: its solubility as a sulfate in water
options.rationale: Many s-block ions form soluble sulfates too.
Hydroxide precipitates form with ions of all kinds of metals.

options.content: its green colour in aqueous solution
options.rationale: Correct: d-d electron transitions absorb visible light.

parts.explanation: Colour arises from electrons moving between split d orbitals, which needs a partly filled d sub-shell.

explanation: X is chromium. Cr³⁺ is [Ar] 3d³ with three unpaired electrons; forming it from Cr(g) needs 5233 kJ mol⁻¹.
hints: A half-filled 3d sub-shell with one 4s electron identifies X.

stem:
Data (textbook values) for potassium, an s-block metal, and copper, a transition metal, both in Period 4:

| property | potassium | copper |
|---|---|---|
| melting point / °C | 63 | 1085 |
| density / g cm⁻³ | 0.86 | 8.96 |
| colour of the sulfate | white | white when anhydrous, blue when hydrated |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Explain why copper has the higher melting point.

points.description: Copper has more delocalised electrons per atom (3d as well as 4s electrons, against one 4s electron for potassium) and smaller, more highly charged cations
So its metallic bonding is stronger and needs more energy to break

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Copper uses 3d as well as 4s electrons in metallic bonding and its cations are smaller and more highly charged, so the attraction between the cations and the delocalised electrons is much stronger than in potassium, which delocalises only one electron per atom.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Explain why copper has the higher density.

points.description: Copper atoms are heavier (Ar 63.5 against 39.1)
Copper atoms are much smaller, so they pack more closely

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Copper atoms have a larger mass and a much smaller radius than potassium atoms, so more mass is packed into each unit volume.

parts.label: (c)
parts.explanation: Cu: [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s¹ (full 3d is more stable); Cu²⁺ loses 4s¹ and one 3d electron: 3d⁹.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: The first two ionisation energies of copper are 745 and 1960 kJ mol⁻¹. Calculate the energy, in kJ mol⁻¹, needed to form Cu²⁺(g) from Cu(g).

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Copper(II) sulfate is paramagnetic, but potassium sulfate is not.
parts.explanation: True: Cu²⁺ (3d⁹) has one unpaired electron; K⁺ has none.

parts.label: (f)
parts.stem: Hydrated copper(II) sulfate is blue, but potassium sulfate and copper(I) compounds such as copper(I) iodide are white. Use electron configurations to explain the difference.

points.description: K⁺ has the argon configuration with no d electrons, so no d-d transition is possible (white)
Cu²⁺ is 3d⁹: a partly filled d sub-shell
In hydrated copper(II) sulfate the water ligands split the d orbitals, so an electron can absorb visible light and move to a higher d orbital: the compound is coloured
Cu⁺ is 3d¹⁰: the d sub-shell is full, so no d-d transition is possible and no visible light is absorbed (white)

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: K⁺ has no d electrons, so potassium sulfate cannot absorb visible light by a d-d transition and is white. Cu²⁺ is [Ar] 3d⁹. Water ligands split its d orbitals, and an electron can absorb visible light to move into the higher, partly empty level, so the compound is coloured. Cu⁺ is [Ar] 3d¹⁰; every d orbital is full, so there is no d-d transition and copper(I) iodide is white.

explanation: Copper: stronger metallic bonding, heavier and smaller atoms; Cu²⁺ (3d⁹) is coloured and paramagnetic, Cu⁺ (3d¹⁰) is colourless.
hints: Think about bonding for melting point and about mass and size for density.
Colour needs a partly filled d sub-shell.
